title: Los Angeles in the Depression and Lionel Hampton's Culver City band
summary: He played the Irving Brothers' Palomino dance hall at ten cents a dance, then Hampton's band with Herschel Evans; Hampton would not allow whistling.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Yes, and during that time there was other bands, other Mexican bands and and Black bands and a . . . In all the different theaters -- there was a Rube Wolfe at the Paramount that had a band there. And . . .
What about the Spike Brothers? The Spike Brothers?

The Spike Bro -- no, I didn't see the Spike Brothers. I -- they, they weren't -- I don't believe they were -- I can't recall -- now maybe they were still there -- they were there, but I never got a chance to see them. Anyway, that a -- in Los Angeles the jazz, the jazz business was pretty, pretty good, and we -- I made a nice little living with the Max Melody Makers band, and pretty soon I, I worked in the -- with the Irving Brothers in, in the, the Palomino Dance Hall. And it was ten cents a dance then. At that time I was makin' 12 bucks-a-week which was great money during those years. That was a depression, and I had a car, and, oh, I was raisin' cane this time. Finally, finally I got in with Lionel Hampton, and this was long before he was known. And he had a band at the Culver City, and in that band I remember Hershel Evans. What a beautiful tenor player he was! And a trumpet player by the name of Red
Mack, and Gladys was in charge of the band. I remember you couldn't whees, whistle in Lionel's dressing room. So . . .
He don't like -- he was superstitious a bit like that.
